theirs: Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is the heart of Islam: 'Say: He is Allah, the One; Allah, the Eternal Refuge; He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent' (Quran 112:1-4). Associating partners with Allah (shirk) is the one sin Allah will not forgive if a person dies upon it (Quran 4:48). Allah is utterly unlike His creation — 'there is nothing like unto Him' (Quran 42:11) — and is known through His most beautiful names and attributes (Quran 7:180). The classic Sunni creed Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah opens here: Allah is one, without partner, and nothing is like Him.
bible: Christianity equally confesses one God — 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one' (Deuteronomy 6:4) — while holding that the one God eternally exists as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one Being, three persons (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14). The Word who was 'with God' and 'was God' became flesh in Jesus (John 1:1, 14). This is not three gods; the Nicene Creed begins 'We believe in one God,' and historic Christianity has always condemned tritheism.
key: Both faiths confess exactly one God; the divide is whether His oneness is an absolute singularity (tawhid) or an eternal tri-personal unity (Trinity).

theirs: Isa ibn Maryam is one of the greatest messengers of Allah, born of the virgin Maryam by Allah's creative command 'Be' (Quran 3:45-47; 19:19-21), honored as al-Masih (the Messiah), 'a word from Allah,' and 'a spirit from Him' (Quran 4:171) — yet a servant and prophet, not divine and not the son of God (Quran 5:75; 112:3). He performed miracles by Allah's permission, including healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead (Quran 3:49). He was neither killed nor crucified — 'it was made to appear so to them' — and Allah raised him alive to Himself (Quran 4:157-158). He will return before the Hour (Quran 43:61).
bible: Jesus is fully God and fully man: 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us' (John 1:14), and 'in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily' (Colossians 2:9). He was crucified for sins, buried, and raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4), his death a voluntary ransom (Mark 10:45; Romans 5:8). The apostles confessed him as Lord and God (John 20:28), and his cross and resurrection are the center of the Christian gospel, not an embarrassment to be denied.
key: The crux is whether Jesus is a revered human prophet who was never crucified, or the incarnate Son of God whose crucifixion and resurrection accomplish salvation.

theirs: Ruh al-Qudus ('the Holy Spirit') in the Quran is, in the majority Sunni tafsir, the angel Jibril (Gabriel): Allah strengthened Isa with Ruh al-Qudus (Quran 2:87; 5:110), and Ruh al-Qudus 'brought the Quran down from your Lord in truth' (Quran 16:102), where he is also called 'the Trustworthy Spirit' (Quran 26:193). Angels are honored servants created by Allah who never disobey Him (Quran 21:26-27; 66:6). The Spirit is therefore a creature and messenger of Allah, and directing worship to him would be shirk.
bible: The Holy Spirit is a divine person, not an angel: he spoke through the prophets (2 Peter 1:21), lying to him is lying to God (Acts 5:3-4), and he is named alongside the Father and the Son in baptism (Matthew 28:19). Jesus promised him as 'another Helper' who teaches, convicts, and abides with believers forever (John 14:16-17, 26). He personally indwells every Christian (Romans 8:9-11), which is why Christians worship and pray in the Spirit rather than merely about him.
key: The question is whether 'the Holy Spirit' names the created angel Gabriel who carries revelation, or the third divine person of the Trinity who indwells believers.

theirs: The Quran is the literal, uncreated speech of Allah, revealed to Muhammad through Jibril over twenty-three years, inimitable (Quran 2:23) and divinely guaranteed against corruption: 'Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and We will surely preserve it' (Quran 15:9). Earlier scriptures — the Tawrat, Zabur, and Injil — were genuine revelations, but Muslims hold their present texts suffered alteration (tahrif; cf. Quran 2:79), so the Quran confirms what is true in them and stands as the final criterion over them (Quran 5:48). The Prophet's sunnah, preserved in authenticated hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim), is the second source of authority, for obeying the Messenger is obeying Allah (Quran 4:80; 59:7).
bible: The Bible, Old and New Testaments, is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), written by men 'carried along by the Holy Spirit' (2 Peter 1:21). Jesus taught that Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35) and that heaven and earth will pass away before his words do (Matthew 24:35); 'the word of our God will stand forever' (Isaiah 40:8). Historic Christianity therefore denies that the biblical text was lost or corrupted, holding it to be the sufficient and final written authority, needing no superseding revelation.
key: The crux is whether the Bible's text stands preserved and final, or was corrupted in transmission and superseded by the Quran as God's protected last word.

theirs: Salvation comes through iman (faith in Allah and His Messenger) joined with righteous deeds and, above all, Allah's mercy: on the Day of Judgment, those whose scales weigh heavy with good succeed (Quran 23:102-103; 101:6-9). The five pillars — shahada, salah, zakat, sawm, and hajj — form the framework of the faithful life (Sahih al-Bukhari 8). Sincere tawbah (repentance) erases sin (Quran 39:53; 25:70), and the Prophet taught that no one enters Paradise by deeds alone, but only when Allah covers him with mercy (Sahih al-Bukhari 5673; Sahih Muslim 2816). No atoning mediator is needed or possible — 'no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another' (Quran 35:18) — for each soul answers to Allah directly.
bible: Salvation is by grace through faith, 'not a result of works, so that no one may boast' (Ephesians 2:8-9): all have sinned, and all who believe are 'justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus' (Romans 3:23-24). Christ bore sins in the sinner's place — 'he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree' (1 Peter 2:24; Isaiah 53:5-6). Good works necessarily follow as the fruit of salvation, not its ground (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17).
key: The crux is whether one is saved by faith, deeds, and mercy weighed at the final judgment, or by trusting an atonement Christ has already accomplished on one's behalf.

theirs: Every child is born upon the fitra — an innate, pure disposition to recognize and worship Allah alone (Quran 30:30; Sahih al-Bukhari 1358) — and no one inherits Adam's sin: Adam repented, and Allah accepted his repentance completely (Quran 2:37; 20:122). Humans are created morally accountable but weak and forgetful (Quran 4:28), and sin consists of individual acts, not a corrupted nature; 'no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another' (Quran 35:18). The remedy for sin is remembrance, obedience, and repentance — 'all the children of Adam are sinners, and the best of sinners are those who repent' (Jami at-Tirmidhi 2499).
bible: Humanity is made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), yet 'sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men' (Romans 5:12). David confesses, 'in sin did my mother conceive me' (Psalm 51:5), and 'the heart is deceitful above all things' (Jeremiah 17:9). Because the problem is a fallen nature and not only wrong acts, Jesus says one 'must be born again' (John 3:3) — humanity needs regeneration, not merely reminding.
key: The crux is whether humans are born pure upon a God-ward fitra and merely commit sins, or are born with a fallen nature that requires new birth.

theirs: At death the soul enters barzakh, the intervening realm lasting until the resurrection — 'behind them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected' (Quran 23:100) — where the grave brings questioning by the angels and either bliss or punishment; Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah affirms the punishment of the grave as orthodox belief. On the Day of Judgment all are raised, the scales of deeds are set (Quran 21:47), records are given, and souls pass to Jannah — gardens beneath which rivers flow (Quran 2:25; Surah 55-56) — or to Jahannam, the Fire (Quran 3:185; 67:6-11). Muslims who enter the Fire for their sins may later be brought out by Allah's mercy and the Prophet's intercession (shafa'a; Sahih al-Bukhari 7439), but one who dies upon shirk is barred from Paradise forever (Quran 4:48; 5:72).
bible: At death the believer goes to be with Christ — 'away from the body and at home with the Lord' (2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43). All will be bodily raised, 'those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment' (John 5:28-29). The final states are everlasting: God dwelling with his redeemed in a renewed creation (Revelation 21:3-4), and eternal punishment for the lost (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 20:15), with destiny turning on one's standing in Christ (John 3:36).
key: The crux is whether final destiny is settled by the weighing of deeds — with possible release from the Fire for believers — or fixed at death by one's relationship to Christ.

theirs: The believer lives between fear and hope (khawf and raja) — fearing Allah's justice while trusting His mercy, for 'do not despair of the mercy of Allah' (Quran 39:53) yet His punishment is real (Quran 15:49-50). Sunni orthodoxy holds that no one may declare his own final destiny, since one's ending (khatima) is known to Allah alone; even the Prophet said, 'None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds... not even me, unless Allah covers me with His mercy' (Sahih al-Bukhari 5673; Sahih Muslim 2816). Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah teaches that we do not testify of any specific member of the qiblah that he is in the Garden or the Fire. Claiming certainty of Paradise is presumption; despairing of mercy is itself a sin (Quran 12:87) — the exceptions are those, like the ten Companions, named by revelation itself.
bible: Assurance of salvation is presented as normal Christian experience: 'I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life' (1 John 5:13). Jesus promises his sheep 'will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand' (John 10:28), and 'there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus' (Romans 8:1), from whose love nothing can separate the believer (Romans 8:38-39). This confidence rests on Christ's finished work rather than the believer's own merit.
key: The crux is whether a believer can presently know his final salvation, or must rightly remain between fear and hope because the outcome is Allah's alone to know.

theirs: Allah sent a messenger to every nation with the same message — 'worship Allah and shun false gods' (Quran 16:36) — from Adam through Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, and Isa, all of whom submitted to Allah. Muhammad is the last of them, 'the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets' (Quran 33:40), sent 'as a mercy to the worlds' (Quran 21:107), and his sunnah is the beautiful pattern for life (Quran 33:21). Sunni theology holds that prophets possess isma — protection from major sin and from error in delivering revelation. The Prophet is loved and obeyed as part of faith itself (Quran 3:31-32), yet he is a man and servant of Allah, never an object of worship.
bible: God 'spoke to our fathers by the prophets' but 'in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son' (Hebrews 1:1-2) — Jesus is the one to whom all prophecy pointed (Luke 24:27), and the apostolic witness to him completes the foundation (Ephesians 2:20). Christians are commanded to test every later claim of revelation (1 John 4:1) and to receive no other gospel, 'even if we or an angel from heaven' should preach it (Galatians 1:8). Historic Christianity therefore recognizes no prophet after the apostles who revises the gospel of Christ.
key: The crux is whether God's revelation culminates in Muhammad as the final prophet, or in Jesus as the Son beyond whom no further prophet can speak a new word.

theirs: Salah — the five daily prescribed prayers (fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha) — is the second pillar of Islam, performed in Arabic, facing the qibla toward the Ka'bah (Quran 2:144), after wudu, ritual purification (Quran 5:6), in fixed cycles (rak'at) of standing, bowing, and prostration with recitation of Surah al-Fatiha in every unit (Sahih al-Bukhari 756). It is commanded directly — 'establish prayer for My remembrance' (Quran 20:14) — and is the first deed a servant is questioned about on the Day of Judgment (Jami at-Tirmidhi 413). Alongside salah, the Muslim offers du'a — personal supplication in any language, at any time (Quran 40:60) — and dhikr, the remembrance of Allah.
bible: Christian prayer is addressed to God as Father, in the name of the Son (Matthew 6:9-13; John 14:13-14), with no prescribed hours, direction, ritual washing, or sacred language. Believers are told to 'pray without ceasing' (1 Thessalonians 5:17) and to 'draw near with confidence to the throne of grace' through Christ the high priest (Hebrews 4:16). True worship is 'in spirit and truth' rather than tied to a place (John 4:23-24), though Christians have always also gathered for corporate, ordered worship (Acts 2:42).
key: The crux is whether worship centers on divinely prescribed ritual prayer at set times in set form, or on continual, free access to God as Father through Christ.

theirs: Allah's guidance embraces all of life through the sharia, drawn from the Quran and sunnah and elaborated by the science of fiqh in the established madhhabs, classifying actions from obligatory (fard) to forbidden (haram). Daily practice includes eating only halal food and avoiding pork and intoxicants (Quran 2:173; 5:3, 90-91), shunning riba — interest (Quran 2:275) — and observing modesty in dress and conduct for both men and women (Quran 24:30-31). Living within the law is itself worship and the path of taqwa: 'This day I have perfected for you your religion' (Quran 5:3). The law is a mercy, not a burden — 'Allah intends for you ease, and does not intend hardship' (Quran 2:185).
bible: The moral law is summed up in love for God and neighbor (Matthew 22:37-40), and 'Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes' (Romans 10:4). The ceremonial and dietary codes no longer bind: Jesus 'declared all foods clean' (Mark 7:18-19; Acts 10:15), and believers are told, 'for freedom Christ has set us free' — a freedom used to serve one another in love (Galatians 5:1, 13). In disputable matters, each is governed by conscience before the Lord (Romans 14:5-6).
key: The crux is whether the godly life is walked inside a comprehensive revealed legal code, or in Spirit-led liberty of conscience under the law of love.

theirs: Marriage (nikah) is a solemn covenant (Quran 4:21) and a beloved sunnah of the Prophet (Sunan Ibn Majah 1846); spouses are 'garments for one another' (Quran 2:187), created so that hearts find tranquility, love, and mercy (Quran 30:21). The husband bears responsibility for provision and maintenance of the family (Quran 4:34), while the mahr (dower) is the wife's own inalienable right (Quran 4:4). A man may marry up to four wives on condition of just treatment — with the warning that justice is hard to achieve (Quran 4:3, 129) — and Muslim men may marry chaste women of the People of the Book (Quran 5:5). Divorce is lawful but regulated with waiting periods and due process (Quran 2:229-232), and children owe lifelong kindness to their parents (Quran 17:23-24).
bible: Marriage was instituted by God at creation as one man and one woman becoming 'one flesh' (Genesis 2:24), a union Jesus declared permanent: 'what God has joined together, let not man separate' (Matthew 19:4-6). It is a living picture of Christ and the church, with husbands commanded to love their wives sacrificially 'as Christ loved the church' (Ephesians 5:25, 31-32), and spouses giving themselves mutually (1 Corinthians 7:3-4). Monogamy is the creational pattern and the New Testament norm (1 Timothy 3:2), and children are to be raised 'in the discipline and instruction of the Lord' (Ephesians 6:1-4).
key: The crux is whether marriage is a contract within revealed law that permits conditional polygyny, or a lifelong one-flesh union of two that images Christ and the church.

theirs: Belief in qadar — Allah's decree of all things, the good of it and the bad of it — is the sixth article of iman, established in the hadith of Jibril (Sahih Muslim 8). 'Indeed, We created all things with qadar' (Quran 54:49), and everything that will occur was written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) before creation (Quran 57:22). Yet humans genuinely earn their deeds and are justly accountable — 'whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve' (Quran 18:29) — for Allah wrongs no one (Quran 4:40); Ash'ari theology names this human share kasb (acquisition). Sunni orthodoxy holds decree and responsibility together, rejecting both fatalism (Jabriyya) and denial of decree (Qadariyya), and Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah counsels that the depths of qadar are Allah's secret, not to be over-probed.
bible: God 'works all things according to the counsel of his will' (Ephesians 1:11): 'the heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps' (Proverbs 16:9), and those he foreknew he predestined, called, justified, and glorified (Romans 8:29-30). Yet Scripture equally issues real commands and real choices — 'choose this day whom you will serve' (Joshua 24:15) — and holds every person accountable (Acts 17:30-31). Historic Christianity affirms both truths, locating sovereignty in the Father's redemptive purpose in Christ, while its traditions (Augustinian/Reformed and Arminian among them) have long debated the balance.
key: Both traditions hold divine sovereignty together with human accountability; the crux is that Islam rests this in an eternally written decree received as Allah's inscrutable secret, while Christian teaching anchors it in God's fatherly purpose worked out in Christ.

theirs: Sunni eschatology, drawn chiefly from hadith, expects the signs of the Hour to multiply until the Mahdi — a rightly-guided leader from the Prophet's family — appears and fills the earth with justice as it was filled with oppression (Sunan Abi Dawud 4282-4285). Then comes the Dajjal, the one-eyed false messiah and greatest trial ever to face mankind (Sahih Muslim 2934; Sahih al-Bukhari 7131), after which Isa ibn Maryam will descend — in the well-known narration, at the white minaret east of Damascus (Sahih Muslim 2937) — kill the Dajjal, break the cross, and rule justly by Islam (Sahih al-Bukhari 3448); the Quran calls Isa a sign of the Hour (Quran 43:61). Gog and Magog (Yajuj and Majuj) will then be released (Quran 21:96) before the trumpet, resurrection, and judgment. (Twelver Shia Islam diverges here, identifying the Mahdi as the Twelfth Imam, alive in occultation.)
bible: Christ will return personally, visibly, and in glory — 'this Jesus... will come in the same way as you saw him go' (Acts 1:11; Matthew 24:30) — the dead will be raised and all judged (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17; Revelation 20:11-15). Before the end comes a great deception under the 'man of lawlessness' or antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:3-8; 1 John 2:18), whom Christ destroys at his appearing. History ends not in another era of earthly rule but in new heavens and a new earth where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:1-4); the day and hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36).
key: Both faiths await Jesus's return and a final deceiver; the crux is what Jesus returns as — in Islam a Muslim prophet who vindicates tawhid and Islam, in Christianity the divine Lord who raises the dead and judges the world.
